en: So complex or deep that few people can grasp it
hook: ABSTRUSE: ABSTRACT and CONFUSE.
story: Abstruse. On the first day of a quantum mechanics course, a visiting professor filled four whiteboards with symbols, spoke of Hilbert spaces and eigenstates, and never once gave an example. By the end, even the top students were staring blankly. Kamal whispered to Rafi, "The only word I understood was hello." The lecture was abstruse: difficult to understand, obscure. In Latin, abstrusus means hidden away. Do not confuse it with obtuse, meaning slow witted. Synonyms: recondite, esoteric, arcane.

gre.s: Although the philosopher's early essays were lucid and accessible, his later work grew so ____ that even specialists confessed they could not follow its arguments.
gre.clue: even specialists confessed they could not follow its arguments

example: Rahim gave up on the abstruse tax manual and simply asked an accountant in Motijheel to fill in his return.

en: Excessively eager to acquire money or possessions
hook: ACQUISITIVE: always ACQUIRING more.
story: Acquisitive. Mr. Haque already owned three flats in Gulshan, two cars, and a shop in a busy market. Yet every weekend he went hunting for another plot of land, another apartment, another bargain. His children joked that he could not see anything without wanting to own it. He was deeply acquisitive: excessively eager to acquire money or possessions. The word comes from acquire, to get. An acquisitive society judges people by what they own. Synonyms: grasping, avaricious, covetous.

gre.s: Far from being content with his considerable wealth, the tycoon remained relentlessly ____, buying up rival companies merely to add them to his holdings.
gre.clue: buying up rival companies merely to add them to his holdings

example: In an acquisitive age, the monk's tiny room with one blanket and a few books struck visitors as a quiet rebuke.

en: To persuade someone through flattery or gentle, persistent coaxing
bn: তোষামোদ করে রাজি করানো; ভুলিয়ে-ভালিয়ে রাজি করানো
hook: CAJOLE: CAGE them with sweet words, JOLLY them along.
story: Cajole. Little Tania wanted ice cream before dinner, and her father said no. So she climbed onto his lap, told him he was the best father in Bangladesh, rubbed his tired shoulders, and asked sweetly, again and again, for just one small cone. Twenty minutes later they were walking to the shop. She had cajoled him: persuaded him through flattery and gentle, persistent coaxing. Cajole and wheedle are near twins. Synonyms: coax, sweet-talk.

gre.s: Unable to force the stubborn witness to testify, the detective tried instead to ____ him, offering compliments and small favors until he agreed to talk.
gre.clue: offering compliments and small favors

example: Sadia cajoled her little brother into finishing his homework by promising him an extra hour of football.

en: Rude and bad-tempered in a mean-spirited way
hook: CHURLISH: a grumpy CHURL who growls at everyone.
story: Churlish. Tanvir's friends secretly planned a birthday party for him: balloons, cake, and a slideshow of embarrassing photos. When he walked in and everyone shouted "Surprise!", he frowned. "I hate surprises." He ate one slice of cake, thanked nobody, and left after ten minutes. His friends were stunned. His behaviour was churlish: rude, bad-tempered, and ungracious. It would be churlish to refuse a sincere gift. A churl was once a rude peasant.

gre.s: It would be ____ to criticize the volunteers' modest fundraiser, given how generously they had donated their own time.
gre.clue: given how generously they had donated their own time

example: The guest's churlish refusal to thank his hosts for the elaborate wedding feast embarrassed his entire family.

en: Sad and disappointed
hook: CREST-FALLEN: a rooster whose proud crest has drooped.
story: Crestfallen. Tanvir had studied for eight months for the scholarship exam. When the results were posted, he searched the list three times. His name was not there. He had missed the cut-off by two marks. He walked out with his head down, shoulders slumped, unable to speak. He was crestfallen: sad and deeply disappointed. Picture a proud rooster whose bright crest has suddenly drooped. It is the opposite of elated.

gre.s: The usually confident candidate looked ____ as the results came in, his campaign having fallen far short of expectations.
gre.clue: having fallen far short of expectations

example: Imran looked crestfallen when the publisher returned his first manuscript with a polite but firm rejection letter.

en: Cheerful and full of energy; bubbling with enthusiasm
hook: EBULLIENT: BUBBLING over like boiling water.
story: Ebullient. Mehjabin had been rejected by five universities. Then one morning an email arrived: a full scholarship to study in Canada. She ran through the hostel shouting, hugged the cook, called her mother, and danced on the roof. For the rest of the week she was ebullient: cheerful, full of energy, bubbling over with enthusiasm. Ebullient literally means boiling up, from Latin bullire, to boil. Picture happiness bubbling over a pot. Synonyms: exuberant, buoyant, effervescent. Opposite: morose.

gre.s: Normally reserved and soft-spoken, the professor was uncharacteristically ____ at the reception, laughing loudly and greeting every guest with a warm embrace.
gre.clue: laughing loudly and greeting every guest with a warm embrace

example: The ebullient fans poured into the streets of Chattogram, dancing and waving flags after the late winning goal.

en: Worthy of great respect
hook: ESTIMABLE: held in high ESTEEM.
story: Estimable. For forty years, Dr Tania Rahman ran a free clinic in a remote char village, treating thousands of patients and refusing every offer of a city job. When she retired, the whole district came to thank her. She was an estimable woman: worthy of great respect. Estimable shares a root with esteem, so think of someone held in high esteem. On the GRE it rarely means able to be estimated. Synonyms: admirable, respected, worthy.

gre.s: Despite their political differences, even the senator's rivals regarded him as thoroughly ____, a public servant whose integrity had never once been questioned.
gre.clue: whose integrity had never once been questioned

example: The retiring headmistress was an estimable woman who had taught three generations of the same village families.

en: Quickly fading or disappearing
hook: EVANESCENT: EVAPORATES and VANISHES.
story: Evanescent. After a sudden shower over the Padma, a rainbow arched across the sky, so bright it seemed painted. Arif scrambled for his phone. By the time he unlocked it, the colours were already fading. By the time he opened the camera, the sky was plain grey again. The rainbow had been evanescent: quickly fading and disappearing. Think: it evaporates and vanishes. Evanescent, ephemeral, and transient all describe things that do not last.

gre.s: The perfume's scent proved ____, fading within minutes of being applied despite the manufacturer's promise that it would last all day.
gre.clue: fading within minutes

example: Social media fame is often evanescent, and last month's viral singer may already be forgotten by her followers.

en: Needing to be dealt with right away
hook: EXIGENT: an EMERGENT, EXTREME need.
story: Exigent. At two in the morning, the river embankment near Sirajganj began to give way. Water was seeping through, and three villages lay behind it. There was no time for meetings or permits; volunteers grabbed sandbags in the dark. The situation was exigent: pressing, demanding immediate action. The noun is exigency, an urgent need. Exigent can also describe a demanding person, like an exigent boss who wants everything yesterday. Synonyms: urgent, pressing, critical.

gre.s: Because the circumstances were so ____, with the floodwaters rising by the hour, officials bypassed the usual approval process and evacuated the town at once.
gre.clue: with the floodwaters rising by the hour

example: Facing exigent demands from creditors, the small garment factory sold two of its machines to cover the wages.

en: Interchangeable; replaceable by another identical item
hook: FUNGIBLE: FUN to swap, since one is as good as another.
story: Fungible. If Sara lends you a hundred-taka note and you return a different hundred-taka note, she does not mind. Any note is as good as another. But if she lends you her grandmother's wedding ring, you cannot return a different ring, however similar. Money is fungible: interchangeable with any identical item. The ring is not. Rice, oil, and gold are fungible. Artworks, memories, and people are not.

gre.s: Unlike works of art, which are unique, commodities such as wheat are ____: one bushel can be substituted for another without any loss of value.
gre.clue: one bushel can be substituted for another without any loss of value

example: Banknotes are fungible, so it makes no difference which particular thousand-taka note the cashier hands you.

en: Harmful or hostile; tending to obstruct
hook: INIMICAL: contains 'enemy' (inimicus in Latin).
story: Inimical. Tanvir studied until two every night, scrolling his phone in bed afterward. Then he wondered why he forgot words by morning. His doctor explained: blue light and late nights are inimical to good sleep, and poor sleep is inimical to memory. Inimical means harmful or hostile, acting like an enemy. In fact, the word comes from the Latin for enemy. A climate inimical to plant life is one where nothing can grow.

gre.s: Constant noise and interruptions are ____ to the deep concentration that serious writing demands.
gre.clue: the deep concentration that serious writing demands

example: Soaring rents in the city center have proved inimical to the small bookshops that once lined the old streets.

en: Untruthfulness; the habit of lying
hook: MENDACITY: MEN DARE lie.
story: Mendacity. A local politician promised a new bridge, then claimed it had been built, then claimed the river had changed course, then blamed the villagers for the delay. Every week brought a new lie. Eventually even his supporters stopped believing anything he said. They were tired of his mendacity: his untruthfulness, his habit of lying. Do not confuse mendacity, lying, with mendicancy, begging. The adjective is mendacious. Synonyms: dishonesty, deceit, duplicity. Opposite: veracity.

gre.s: The memoir was celebrated as a model of candor until journalists exposed its author's ____: many of its most moving episodes had simply been invented.
gre.clue: many of its most moving episodes had simply been invented

example: Once the auditors revealed the chairman's mendacity, shareholders demanded to know how many earlier reports had been invented.

en: Someone who commits crimes or misbehaves
hook: MIS-CREANT: a MIS-CREATED person who does wrong.
story: Miscreant. Every night for a month, someone slashed the tyres of motorcycles parked outside Rafi's building. The guards were puzzled and the residents furious, until a hidden camera caught the culprit: a teenager from the next street who did it for fun. The police called him a miscreant: a person who behaves badly or breaks the law. Bangladeshi newspapers often use the word for unidentified criminals. Mis means wrong. Synonyms: wrongdoer, villain, delinquent.

gre.s: The townspeople regarded the young man as a hopeless ____ until he returned the stolen money and spent years volunteering to repay his debt to the community.
gre.clue: returned the stolen money

example: Security cameras finally caught the miscreants who had been slashing bicycle tires outside the university hostel.

en: Fashionable; stylish
hook: MODISH: MODERN and in MODE (fashion).
story: Modish. Last winter, every young person in Dhanmondi seemed to wear the same oversized hoodie; this year it is handloom kurtas with white sneakers. Nabila's cousin Tisha follows each trend the moment it appears online. Her style is modish: fashionable and stylish. Modish comes from mode, as in a la mode, meaning in the current fashion. It can sound slightly mocking, hinting at a trend that will not last. Synonyms: fashionable, trendy, voguish. Opposites: outmoded, dowdy.

gre.s: The restaurant's décor, so ____ when it opened a decade ago, now looks hopelessly dated, a relic of a style no one wants anymore.
gre.clue: now looks hopelessly dated

example: In the 1960s, modish young women in Dhaka wore bouffant hairstyles copied from the posters of popular film stars.

en: Too eager to please or obey; excessively flattering
hook: OBSEQUIOUS: 'obsessively SEEK to please us'.
story: Obsequious. Whenever the manager walked past, Babu jumped to his feet. "Sir! Lovely tie, sir! Tea, sir? Your idea this morning was brilliant, sir!" He laughed at the manager's jokes before the punchline. He agreed before the manager finished speaking. His colleagues rolled their eyes. Obsequious means far too eager to please and obey, flattering in a way that feels fake. Think: obsessively seeking approval. It is the opposite of independent and self-respecting.

gre.s: The courtiers' ____ praise of the king, which never wavered even when his decrees were absurd, revealed more fear than admiration.
gre.clue: never wavered even when his decrees were absurd

example: The new manager grew tired of the obsequious clerk who agreed with every remark and laughed at every joke.

en: Serving as a typical or perfect example of something
hook: PARADIGM = a model. PARADIGMATIC = the model example.
story: Paradigmatic. When business professors want to explain how a startup can change a country, they often tell the story of bKash: a simple idea, a huge unmet need, and explosive growth until millions of people sent money by phone. It is the textbook example. It is paradigmatic: serving as a perfect, typical model of its kind. A paradigm is a model or pattern. Paradigmatic is a fancier cousin of quintessential.

gre.s: The trial has become ____, cited in nearly every textbook as the classic example of judicial overreach.
gre.clue: the classic example

example: For many economists, the rise of the garment industry is the paradigmatic case of export-led growth in a poor country.

en: Very reluctant to spend money; tight with cash
hook: PARSIMONIOUS: PARSING every penny, unwilling to spend.
story: Parsimonious. Uncle Kamal is rich. But he reuses tea bags three times, refuses to turn on the ceiling fan in summer, walks forty minutes to save a ten-taka rickshaw fare, and gives his grandchildren exactly two taka each on Eid. When his son asked for money for medicine, he asked for receipts first. He is parsimonious: extremely unwilling to spend money, stingy. Think: parsing every penny. It is the opposite of prodigal and extravagant.

gre.s: The billionaire was so ____ that he installed pay phones in his mansion so that guests would have to pay for their own calls.
gre.clue: installed pay phones in his mansion

example: The parsimonious landlord refused to replace a single broken bulb in the stairwell, so tenants climbed in darkness.

en: A remark used too often to be interesting or meaningful
hook: PLATITUDE: a FLAT attitude remark; flat, dull, overused.
story: Platitude. When Kamal failed his driving test, everyone had something to say. "Everything happens for a reason." "Failure is the key to success." "Just stay positive." "Tomorrow is another day." Each sentence was meant to comfort him. None of them helped at all. They were platitudes: remarks used so often that they have become dull and meaningless. Think: a flat attitude. Political speeches are often full of platitudes.

gre.s: The commencement speaker disappointed the graduates by offering nothing but ____, urging them to follow their dreams and never give up.
gre.clue: urging them to follow their dreams and never give up

example: When the coach offered only the platitude that winning is not everything, the defeated players rolled their eyes.

en: Easily bent; easily influenced
hook: PLIANT: PLIABLE, bends easily.
story: Pliant. Young bamboo in Bandarban bends almost to the ground in a cyclone, then springs back upright, unbroken, when the wind stops. It is pliant: easily bent without breaking. The new committee members were pliant too, agreeing to whatever the chairman proposed, never pushing back. Pliant means flexible physically, or easily influenced. Synonyms: pliable, malleable, tractable. The opposite is rigid or obstinate.

gre.s: The dictator surrounded himself with ____ advisers who never challenged his decisions, however reckless.
gre.clue: who never challenged his decisions

example: Weavers soak the cane strips overnight until they become pliant enough to be bent into baskets without cracking.

en: A person with expert knowledge in many subjects
hook: POLY = many, MATH = learning. Learned in many things.
story: Polymath. Rabindranath Tagore wrote poetry, novels, and plays, composed over two thousand songs, painted thousands of pictures, founded a university, and debated science with Einstein. Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa, designed flying machines, and studied human anatomy. Both were polymaths: people with expert knowledge in many different fields. Poly means many, math means learning. A polymath does not just dabble; they master.

gre.s: A true ____, she published influential papers in physics, composed music, and wrote two acclaimed novels.
gre.clue: published influential papers in physics, composed music, and wrote two acclaimed novels

example: Rabindranath Tagore was a polymath who wrote novels, composed thousands of songs, painted, and founded a university.

en: To be a sign or warning that something, usually bad, is likely to happen
hook: PORTEND: POR-TEND, a portent, an omen of what's coming.
story: Portend. The fishermen of Kuakata know the signs. When dark clouds gather over the bay, when the birds suddenly fall silent, and when the sea turns an odd copper colour, a storm is coming. They pull their boats onto the shore and tie them down. These signs portend danger: they warn that something, usually bad, is about to happen. A portent is an omen. Falling sales may portend trouble for a company.

gre.s: Economists worry that the sudden drop in consumer spending may ____ a deeper recession in the coming year.
gre.clue: a deeper recession in the coming year

example: Several resignations from the board in one week portended trouble for the struggling airline.

en: To hint that something, often bad, is coming; such a hint
hook: PRE-SAGE: a SAGE who tells the future BEFORE it happens.
story: Presage. Every April, when the first kalbaishakhi storm rumbles across the sky, Joya's mother rushes to bring in the drying clothes, and farmers begin to worry about their ripening rice. The sudden dark wind presages the rough season ahead: it is a sign of what is coming. As a noun, a presage is an omen. The Latin root means to perceive beforehand, to sense the future. A rising temperature can presage illness. Synonyms: portend, foreshadow, herald.

gre.s: Some economists warned that the sudden drop in consumer spending could ____ a deeper recession, while others insisted it was merely a seasonal fluctuation.
gre.clue: while others insisted it was merely a seasonal fluctuation

example: The first cuckoo calls in the mango groves presage the arrival of spring in rural Bengal.

en: Showing unhealthy curiosity about sex or scandal
hook: PRURIENT: like an ITCH (prurire = to itch) for scandal.
story: Prurient. When a famous actor was hospitalized, some tabloids printed almost nothing about his health. Instead, they ran pages of gossip about his secret romances, with blurry photos taken through windows. Readers bought every copy. The tabloids fed a prurient interest: an excessive interest in sexual or scandalous matters. Prurient comes from the Latin for itching, so think of an itch for scandal. Its opposite is prudish. Synonyms: lewd, salacious, voyeuristic.

gre.s: Critics charged that the documentary, despite its claims to serious journalism, merely catered to viewers' ____ curiosity, lingering on lurid details of the celebrity's private affairs.
gre.clue: lingering on lurid details of the celebrity's private affairs

example: The tabloid's prurient coverage of the actress's divorce sold many copies but told readers nothing worth knowing.

en: Always ready to pick a fight or argue
hook: PUGNACIOUS: ready to throw a PUNCH, like a pug that barks at everyone.
story: Pugnacious. Everyone at the tea stall knew Uncle Selim. Say one wrong word about his cricket team, and he would start shouting. A rickshaw brushed his car? He jumped out with his fists up. Once he argued with a parrot. People learned to agree with him about everything. He was pugnacious: eager and quick to argue, quarrel, or fight. Pugnus is Latin for fist, as in pugilist, a boxer. Picture a tiny pug barking at everyone.

gre.s: The usually ____ senator surprised observers by conceding the point calmly instead of launching into one of his customary attacks.
gre.clue: instead of launching into one of his customary attacks

example: The pugnacious little terrier barked at every delivery van on the street, no matter how large.

en: Formidable, especially as an opponent; worthy of respect
hook: RE-DOUBT-ABLE: you DOUBT you can beat them.
story: Redoubtable. In the chess club at Joya's school, one quiet girl had not lost a game in three years. Seniors avoided playing her, and visiting champions left shaking their heads. She was redoubtable: formidable, especially as an opponent, and worthy of respect. It comes from the Old French redouter, to dread, so a redoubtable person is someone others dread to face. Sports writers love it for a fierce rival team. Synonyms: formidable, fearsome, impressive.

gre.s: Even seasoned lawyers dreaded facing her in court, for she was a ____ advocate whose cross-examinations had demolished countless witnesses.
gre.clue: whose cross-examinations had demolished countless witnesses

example: The visiting team knew they faced a redoubtable bowling attack on the spin-friendly pitch at Mirpur.

en: To turn something over in your mind for a long time
hook: RUMINATE: like a cow chewing cud, chewing a thought over and over.
story: Ruminate. Sitting on the steps of the river ghat at dusk, Tanvir ruminated on his future. Stay in Bangladesh near his family, or go abroad for a better career? He turned the question over and over for hours, chewing on every possibility. To ruminate is to think deeply about something, for a long time. Cows ruminate too: they chew their cud again and again. Too much rumination on past mistakes leads to anxiety.

gre.s: Instead of acting decisively, the general would ____ for days over every decision, by which time the opportunity had usually passed.
gre.clue: Instead of acting decisively

example: Sitting on the rooftop after midnight, Arif ruminated on whether to accept the scholarship that would take him abroad.

en: Clever but deliberately misleading argument
hook: SOPHISTRY: from the SOPHISTS, Greek teachers who could argue anything.
story: Sophistry. Caught looking at notes during an exam, Imran argued that he had not cheated, because the answers were already in his memory and the notes merely reminded him. For a moment it sounded clever, but it was nonsense. His argument was sophistry: clever but deliberately misleading reasoning. The Sophists were ancient Greek teachers accused of training students to win arguments rather than find the truth. Synonyms: casuistry, specious reasoning.

gre.s: The lawyer's defense, though dazzlingly clever, was mere ____: each step seemed logical, yet the argument as a whole was designed to mislead the jury.
gre.clue: designed to mislead the jury

example: The debate judges saw through the team's sophistry, noting that its clever statistics proved nothing about the actual motion.

en: Cloudy or muddy (of liquid); confused
hook: TURBID: TURBulent water, all stirred up.
story: Turbid. After three days of heavy rain, the clear stream behind Joya's school turned thick and brown. Mud, leaves, and silt churned in the water, and nobody could see the fish anymore. The water was turbid: cloudy or muddy. Turbid can also describe confused thought or feeling, as in a turbid argument. It comes from the Latin turba, turmoil, as in turbulent. Do not confuse it with turgid, which means swollen or pompous. Synonyms: murky, muddy, cloudy.

gre.s: Once so clear that visitors could see pebbles three meters down, the lake has become ____ since mining began upstream, its waters now thick with silt.
gre.clue: its waters now thick with silt

example: After the monsoon rains, the Padma runs turbid and brown, carrying tons of sediment toward the Bay of Bengal.

en: Serving as a farewell
hook: VALEDICTORY: say VALE (farewell).
story: Valedictory. On the last day of the academic year, the oldest professor in the department gave one final lecture before retiring. He thanked his students, told stories from forty years in the classroom, and ended with two words: "Go well." It was a valedictory speech: serving as a farewell. In some countries, the top graduating student gives the valedictory address. From Latin vale, farewell, and dicere, to say: saying goodbye. Synonyms: farewell, parting.

gre.s: The retiring minister's ____ speech, delivered on her final day in parliament, graciously thanked even her fiercest opponents for decades of spirited debate.
gre.clue: delivered on her final day in parliament

example: In his valedictory column after forty years at the newspaper, the editor thanked the readers who had argued with him most.

en: The appearance of being true or real
hook: VERI-SIMILI-TUDE: VERY SIMILAR to truth.
story: Verisimilitude. To make a film about the 1971 war, the director filmed in real villages, dressed actors in authentic uniforms, used weapons from the period, and hired old freedom fighters as advisers. When veterans watched the premiere, several of them cried. "That is exactly how it was," one said. The film had verisimilitude: the quality of appearing true or real. Veri means true, simili means similar. Good novels have verisimilitude even when invented.

gre.s: The novel's historical details lend it a striking ____, though every one of its characters is invented.
gre.clue: though every one of its characters is invented

example: To add verisimilitude to the war film, the director cast actual veterans and filmed in the villages where battles had occurred.
